edition.locus: Divine Institutes 7.1 (praemium beatitudinis / caelesti mercede / iudicio dei)

source_text: Bene habet, iacta sunt fundamenta, ut ait eximius orator. uerum nos non fundamenta solum iecimus quae firma et idonea essent operi perferendo, sed magnis robustisque molibus aedificium totum paene usque ad summa perduximus. restat, id quod est multo facilius, uel tegere uel ornare, sine quo tamen priora opera et inutilia sunt et ingrata. nam quid prodest aut falsis religionibus liberari aut intellegere ueram? quid aut uanitatem falsae sapientiae peruidere aut quae sit uera cognoscere? quid, inquam, prodest caelestem illam iustitiam defendere? quid cum magnis difficultatibus cultum dei tenere, quae est summa uirtus, nisi eam diuinum praemium beatitudinis perpetuae subsequatur? de qua nobis est in hoc libro disserendum, ne priora omnia irrita et infructuosa uideantur, si hoc cuius causa illa suscepta sunt incertum relinquamus, ne quis forte arbitretur tantos labores in cassum suscipi, dum eorum caelesti mercede diffidit, quam deus statuit ei qui haec suauia terrae bona prae sola nudaque uirtute contempserit. satis et huic parti faciamus cum testimoniis diuinarum litterarum tum etiam probabilibus argumentis, ut aeque clarum sit et futura praesentibus et diuina terrenis et perpetua breuibus esse anteponenda, quoniam temporalia sunt praemia uitiorum, sempiterna uirtutum. exponam igitur rationem mundi, ut facile possit intellegi et quando et quare sit effectus a deo, quod Plato, qui de mundi fabricatione disseruit, nec scire poterat nec explicare: quippe qui caeleste mysterium, quod non nisi prophetis ac deo docente discitur, ignorabat ideoque in perpetuum dixit esse fabricatum. quod longe secus est, quoniam quidquid est solido et graui corpore ut initium cepit aliquando, ita finem capiat necesse est. nam Aristoteles, qui cum non uideret quemadmodum posset tanta rerum magnitudo interire, et hanc praescriptionem uellet effugere, semper ait fuisse mundum ac semper futurum, prorsus nihil uidit, quia quidquid est necesse est habuerit aliquando principium nec omnino quicquam potest esse nisi coeperit. nam cum terram et aquam et ignem disperire consumi extinguique uideamus, quae sunt utique mundi partes, intellegitur id totum esse mortale cuius sunt membra mortalia. ita fit ut natum sit quidquid potest interire. sed et omne quod sub uisum oculorum uenit, et corporale, ut ait Plato, et solubile sit necesse est. unus igitur Epicurus auctore Democrito ueridicus in hac re fuit, qui ait et ortum aliquando et aliquando esse periturum. nec tamen rationem reddere ullam potuit aut quibus de causis tantum hoc opus aut quo tempore resoluatur. quod quoniam nobis deus reuelauit nec coniecturis id adsequimur sed traditione caelesti, docebimus sedulo, ut tandem studiosis ueritatis appareat non uidisse neque conprehendisse philosophos ueritatem, sed ita leuiter odoratos, ut tamen unde eos odor ille sapientiae tam suauis, tam iucundus adflauerit, nullo modo senserint.. interim necessarium puto admonere lecturos quod haec nostra quae tradimus prauae uitiosaeque mentes aut omnino non intellegent — hebetatur enim acies eorum terrenis cupiditatibus, quae sensus omnes grauant inbecillosque reddunt — aut etiamsi intellegent, dissimulabunt tamen et haec uera esse nolent, quia trahuntur a uitiis et scientes malis suis fauent, quorum suauitate capiuntur, et uirtutis uiam deserunt, cuius acerbitate offenduntur. nam quia auaritia et opum inexplebili quadam siti flagrant, quia non possunt uenditis aut dilargitis quae amant tenui cultu uitam degere, sine dubio malunt id esse fictum quo desideriis suis renuntiare coguntur. item qui libidinum stimulis incitati, ut ait poeta, in furias ignemque ruunt, utique incredibilia nos adferre dicunt, quia uulnerant aures eorum praecepta continentiae, quae illos uoluptatibus suis prohibent quibus animam suam cum corpore adiudicauerunt. qui uero ambitione inflati aut amore potentiae inflammati omne studium suum ad honores adquirendos contulerunt, ne si solem quidem ipsum gestemus in manibus, fidem commodabunt ei doctrinae quae illos iubet omni potentia et honore contempto humiles uiuere atque ita humiles, ut et accipere iniuriam possint et referre nolint, si acceperint. hi sunt homines qui contra ueritatem clausis oculis quoquo modo latrant. qui autem sani erunt, id est non ita uitiis inmersi, ut insanabiles sint, et credent his et libenter accedent, et quaecumque dicimus aperta plana simplicia et, quod maxime opus est, uera et inexpugnabilia illis uidebuntur. nemo uirtuti fauet nisi qui sequi potest, sequi autem non facile est omnibus: ii possunt quos paupertas et rerum indigentia exercuit et capaces uirtutis effecit. nam si uirtus est tolerantia malorum, non capiunt ergo uirtutem qui semper in bonis fuerunt, quia mala neque experti sunt neque ferre possunt adsuetudine ac desiderio bonorum, quae sola nouerunt. eo fit ut pauperes et humiles deo credant facilius, qui sunt expediti, quam diuites, qui sunt inpedimentis pluribus inplicati. immo uero catenati et conpediti seruiunt ad nutum dominae cupiditatis, quae illos inextricabilibus uinculis inretiuit, nec possunt in caelum aspicere, quoniam mens eorum in terram prona humique defixa est. uirtutis autem uia non capit magna onera gestantes: angustus admodum trames est per quem iustitia hominem deducit in caelum, hunc tenere non potest nisi qui fuerit expeditus ac nudus. nam isti locupletes multis et ingentibus sarcinis onerati per uiam mortis incedunt, quae latissima est, quoniam late perditio dominatur. his acerba sunt, his uenena quae deus ad iustitiam praecipit quaeque nos dei magisterio de uirtute ac ueritate disserimus. quibus si repugnare audebunt, hostes se necesse est uirtutis iustitiaeque fateantur. Adgrediar nunc quod superest, ut finis operi possit inponi, id autem superest ut de iudicio dei disseramus: quod tum constituetur, cum dominus noster redierit in terram, ut uni cuique pro merito aut praemium persoluat aut poenam. itaque ut in quarto libro de primo aduentu eius diximus, sic in hoc secundum referemus aduentum, quem Iudaei quoque et confitentur et sperant, sed frustra, quoniam necesse est ad eos consolandos reuertatur ad quos conuocandos prius uenerat. nam qui uiolarunt impie humilem, sentient in potestate uictorem eaque omnia quae legunt et non intellegunt deo repensante patientur, quippe qui peccatis omnibus inquinati et insuper sancto cruore perfusi ab illo ipso cui nefandas manus intulerunt sint ad aeterna supplicia destinati. sed erit nobis contra Iudaeos separata materia, in qua illos erroris et sceleris reuincemus.
pass_a_gloss: Foundations laid — without the divine prize of perpetual bliss the whole building is useless; heavenly wage set for those who scorn sweet earth-goods for bare virtue alone; temporal prizes of vices vs everlasting prizes of virtues; world has beginning and end; vicious minds refuse the hard virtue-path; narrow trail of justice leads to heaven; God's judgment when the Lord returns — reward or punishment by desert; second advent.
pass_b_english: It is well: the foundations have been laid, as the outstanding orator says. But we have not only laid foundations firm and fit to carry the work; with great and sturdy masses we have brought the whole building almost to the summit. What remains — far easier — is to cover or adorn it; yet without that the earlier works are both useless and thankless. For what good is it to be freed from false religions or to understand the true one? What good to see through the vanity of false wisdom or to know what true wisdom is? What good, I say, to defend that heavenly justice? What good to hold the worship of God through great hardships — which is the highest virtue — unless the divine prize of perpetual beatitude follows it? Of that prize we must treat in this book, lest all that went before seem empty and fruitless if we leave uncertain the very thing for whose sake those labors were undertaken, lest anyone think such toils are taken up in vain while he distrusts their heavenly wage, which God has fixed for the one who has despised these sweet goods of earth for the sake of bare and naked virtue alone. Let us do enough for this part too, both with the testimonies of the divine writings and with probable arguments, so that it may be equally clear that future things are to be preferred to present ones, divine to earthly, and perpetual to brief, since the prizes of vices are temporal and those of virtues everlasting. I will therefore set out the account of the world, so that it may easily be understood both when and why it was made by God — which Plato, who treated of the world's fashioning, could neither know nor explain, since he was ignorant of the heavenly mystery learned only from the prophets and from God as teacher, and therefore said the world was fashioned to last forever. That is far otherwise, since whatever exists in solid and heavy body, as it once took a beginning, must likewise take an end. For Aristotle, who, because he did not see how so great a mass of things could perish, and wished to escape this rule, says the world always was and always will be, saw nothing at all, because whatever is must once have had a beginning, and absolutely nothing can be unless it has begun. For when we see earth and water and fire perish, be consumed, and be extinguished — which are surely parts of the world — it is understood that that whole is mortal whose members are mortal. So it comes about that whatever can perish was born. But also everything that comes under the sight of the eyes, being bodily, as Plato says, must also be dissoluble. Epicurus alone, then, with Democritus as author, was truthful in this matter, who says both that it once arose and that it will at some time perish. Yet he could give no account of the causes for which this great work is either dissolved or at what time. Since God has revealed this to us, and we reach it not by conjectures but by heavenly tradition, we will teach carefully, so that at last it may appear to those eager for truth that the philosophers neither saw nor grasped the truth, but only lightly caught its scent, yet in no way sensed from where that scent of wisdom, so sweet, so pleasant, had blown upon them.

Meanwhile I think it necessary to warn those who will read that these things we hand on the depraved and vicious minds will either not understand at all — for their sharpness is blunted by earthly desires, which weigh down all the senses and make them weak — or, even if they understand, they will still dissemble and will not want these things to be true, because they are dragged by vices and, knowing it, favor their own evils, by whose sweetness they are caught, and desert the way of virtue, by whose bitterness they are offended. For because they burn with greed and with a kind of unquenchable thirst for wealth, because they cannot, having sold or given away what they love, live a life of thin worship, they without doubt prefer that to be fiction by which they are forced to renounce their desires. Likewise those who, spurred by the goads of lust, as the poet says, rush into furies and fire, will certainly say we bring unbelievable things, because the precepts of continence wound their ears — precepts that forbid them the pleasures to which they have sentenced their soul together with the body. But those swollen with ambition or inflamed with love of power, who have turned their whole zeal to gaining honors, will not lend faith to that teaching — even if we should carry the sun itself in our hands — which commands them, every power and honor despised, to live humble, and so humble that they can both receive injury and refuse to return it if they have received it. These are the humans who bark against the truth with closed eyes in whatever way they can. But those who will be sound — that is, not so sunk in vices that they are incurable — will both believe these things and gladly approach, and whatever we say will seem to them open, plain, simple, and, what is most needed, true and impregnable. No one favors virtue except one who can follow it, but to follow is not easy for all: those can who have been trained by poverty and lack of things and made capable of virtue. For if virtue is endurance of evils, then those who have always been in goods do not take hold of virtue, because they have neither experienced evils nor can bear them, by habit and longing for goods, which alone they know. Hence it happens that the poor and humble believe God more easily, being unencumbered, than the rich, who are tangled in many hindrances — rather, chained and fettered, they serve at the nod of mistress Desire, who has snared them with inextricable bonds, and they cannot look up to heaven, since their mind is bent to earth and fixed on the ground. But the way of virtue does not take those carrying great loads: the trail is quite narrow by which justice leads a human into heaven; no one can hold it unless he has been unencumbered and bare. For those rich ones, loaded with many huge packs, walk the way of death, which is widest, since ruin rules widely. To these are bitter, to these are poisons, the things God commands toward justice and the things we, by God's teaching, treat concerning virtue and truth. If they dare to fight back against these, they must confess themselves enemies of virtue and justice.

I will now approach what remains, so that an end may be set on the work; and what remains is that we treat of the judgment of God, which will then be established when our Lord has returned to earth, so that he may pay each one according to desert either the prize or the punishment. And so, as in the fourth book we spoke of his first coming, so in this we will report the second coming, which the Jews also both confess and hope for — but in vain, since he must return to console those to whom he first came to call. For those who impiously violated the humble one will feel him the victor in power, and with God paying back they will suffer all those things they read and do not understand, since, stained with all sins and moreover steeped in holy blood, they have been destined to eternal punishments by that very one on whom they laid unspeakable hands. But we will have a separate treatment against the Jews, in which we will convict them of error and crime.

choices.choose: perpetual beatitude as necessary crown of virtue
reject: virtue as its own enough end without heavenly wage
choices.why: Prior books are fruitless unless divine prize follows cult and justice.

reject: wide way of the loaded rich toward death
